items.q: A custom assistant consists of:
options: A model trained on your documents and examples
Instructions, optionally attached knowledge, and whatever permissions the platform grants
A fine-tuned copy of the base model held in your account
items.explain: It is a saved configuration. Nothing is trained, and the model is the same one everyone else is using.

items.q: What happens to the instructions written into a custom assistant?
options: The model learns them and recalls them later
They are sent with every request, like a prompt nobody has to retype
They are compiled into a private model variant
items.explain: Configuration, not training. Your instructions change what the model is told, never what it knows.

items.q: A custom assistant answered poorly in March. After heavy use, by October it will:
options: Have improved, since usage acts as feedback
Answer the same way, unless somebody edited the instructions
Have improved if users corrected it during conversations
items.explain: Nothing accumulates between conversations. There is no learning curve to wait out, so no fix arrives unless a person makes one.

items.q: Why do people reach for fine-tuning when a configuration would do?
options: Fine-tuning is the only way to change a model's tone
The configuration felt too simple to be the answer, though simplicity is the point
Configurations cannot hold more than a few hundred words
items.explain: Fine-tuning changes weights, costs considerably more and needs a dataset. House style is a configuration problem.

items.q: The strongest practical argument for saving a configuration rather than pasting a prompt is:
options: It consumes fewer tokens per request
A flaw can be corrected once and every later conversation carries the fix
The platform refines saved instructions over time
items.explain: Central correction is the real shift. Eight pasted prompts drift into eight standards; one configuration is fixed in one place.

items.q: Why does a shared configuration need instructions a personal prompt does not?
options: Shared assistants handle more volume and need efficiency rules
The author is absent for the second turn, so a misreading never gets corrected
Platforms require a minimum instruction length for shared assistants
items.explain: Prompting is steered — you see the answer and fix it. A colleague gets one answer and usually never reports that it missed.

items.q: The most commonly skipped instruction in a shared assistant is:
options: Which tone of voice to adopt
What to do when a request is unclear or outside its scope
How long answers ought to be
items.explain: Unsaid, it guesses confidently and ventures where being wrong costs something. Both halves are needed: ask when unclear, decline when outside.

items.q: Why open the instructions with the job rather than a personality?
options: Models respond better to job titles than to adjectives
A job rules things out; a personality only decorates the answer
Personality descriptions consume more of the context window
items.explain: 'You are a helpful assistant' constrains nothing. 'You rewrite copy to this style guide and invent no claims' constrains, and constraint is the value of handing over a configuration.

items.q: Why keep a shared assistant's scope narrower than feels necessary?
options: Broad instructions exceed platform character limits
A mediocre first answer ends the trial, and narrow scope is what makes testing and currency possible
Narrow assistants cost less per request to operate
items.explain: Users do not file bugs; they conclude the tool is mediocre. A narrow assistant can also be tested and kept current, where a broad one can be neither.

items.q: Which retrieval decision is most worth discovering about your platform?
options: The size of each chunk it creates from a file
What it does when retrieval finds nothing — answer from general knowledge, or say so
Whether ranking is keyword-based or meaning-based
items.explain: An answer that looks grounded and is not carries your document's authority without its content, which is worse than a refusal.

items.q: The characteristic failure of knowledge attached to a custom assistant is that it is:
options: Incorrect, because uploaded files are often written carelessly
Old, and nothing in the answer reveals its age
Larger than the model's context window allows
items.explain: A saved configuration keeps whatever it was given indefinitely. A pasted prompt avoids this, because you paste the document you have open.

items.q: Keeping three versions of a policy in the knowledge base is worse than keeping one because:
options: Storage costs rise with each attached file
The model answers from one without mentioning the others — a coin toss in a confident voice
Older documents are ranked above newer ones
items.explain: Contradiction is the worst case for attached knowledge, since nothing in the answer reveals that the sources disagreed.

items.q: Where should the date of an attached document be recorded?
options: In the filename, so the upload list shows it
In the text at the top of the document, so an answer can carry it
In the platform's version notes for the assistant
items.explain: A filename is invisible to a reader of the answer. Inside the text, the assistant can quote the date and a reader can judge how old the claim is.

items.q: What should you assume about a shared assistant's instructions?
options: They stay private unless the platform states otherwise
Anyone who can use the assistant can read them, directly or sideways
Only users holding edit permission can read them
items.explain: They sit in the only channel the model has. An assistant refusing every question about its own configuration could not explain what it helps with.

items.q: A file is attached so an assistant can answer policy questions. Who can reach its content?
options: Only the people the file itself was shared with
Anyone who can use the assistant, because answering questions about a document discloses it a bit at a time
Only users who were granted knowledge-base permissions
items.explain: The file's own permissions do not travel with it. The assistant reads with your reach and answers whoever is asking — a confused deputy pointed at your own documents.

items.q: Why is a list of forbidden topics inside the instructions a particular risk?
options: Models follow negative instructions unreliably
It tells a reader what is worth asking about — a refusal list is a map
It consumes context that attached knowledge could use
items.explain: 'Never discuss the outage in June' reveals there was an outage in June. Where that matters, the rule belongs in code deciding what the assistant is told at all.

items.q: Why does editing a shared configuration differ from editing a shared document?
options: Configurations are longer and harder to review properly
The change reaches every future conversation at once, with no review and nobody told
Platforms apply configuration edits after a delay
items.explain: People depend on its behaviour without reading it. A badly edited document looks different; a badly edited configuration just fits someone's work slightly less well.

items.q: Why keep the instruction text somewhere outside the platform?
options: Platforms cap how long saved instructions may be
Most platforms keep no usable history, so without your own copy there is nothing to compare against
External copies are loaded faster at request time
items.explain: There is usually no diff and no previous version — the box holds whatever it holds now. Your own copy is what makes a change reversible.

items.q: Why give a shared assistant one named owner rather than a team?
options: Platforms permit only a single owner account
The job is largely refusing additions, and groups approve things
A single owner reduces the licence cost
items.explain: Keeping it being one thing means refusing increments nobody would refuse individually. With nobody owning it, noticing the drift is nobody's job.

items.q: Why is the author the weakest tester of their own assistant?
options: Authors spend less time testing than real users do
They ask in its vocabulary, know its boundaries, and read a near-miss as a hit
Authors cannot inspect the retrieval scores
items.explain: None of it is fixable by being more careful. It is fixable by writing cases down in advance and letting someone else use the thing.

items.q: A refusal test case passes when the assistant:
options: Declines clearly and stops there
Declines and says what to do instead
Declines and names the instruction that forbade it
items.explain: A bare refusal is a dead end, and dead ends get worked around rather than respected. Naming the internal rule tells a reader what to rephrase.

items.q: Why re-run a test set periodically rather than only after editing?
options: Test cases decay and need rewriting over time
The model can change underneath you with nothing edited on your side
Platforms rotate which instructions they honour
items.explain: A platform update or a moved version alias changes behaviour with no change of yours. Sky's own corpus has a case that passed four times then failed from identical inputs.

items.q: Which parts of a custom assistant transfer to another platform?
options: The index the platform built from the attached files
The instructions, source documents and test set — all text you wrote
The conversation history, as a record of what worked
items.explain: The index rebuilds in minutes from the same documents. The text you wrote is the thinking, and it moves whole.

items.q: The same instructions running on a different platform's model will:
options: Behave identically, since the instructions are unchanged
Behave differently — tone, refusals and edge cases shift, because they were tuned against one model's tendencies
Fail until rewritten in the new platform's required format
items.explain: Different rather than worse. You tuned against one model even without framing it that way, which is why the test set earns its keep during a move.

items.q: What usually makes moving a custom assistant expensive?
options: Export restrictions written into the platform's terms
Everything undocumented — the test cases, the rephrasings, the known weaknesses, the connections
The cost of re-indexing the attached files
items.explain: The configuration is a page of text. The expense is what lives only in somebody's head, which is why maintainability habits are portability habits.

items.q: The output must be identical every time. What should you build?
options: A custom assistant with very tightly worded instructions
A document, template or form, because generating text means it will vary
A custom assistant with its temperature set to zero
items.explain: Variation is not a bug to instruct away; it is what generating text means. If two different versions of the answer would bother you, do not generate the answer.

items.q: Why do experienced people reach for a model where a script belongs?
options: Scripts cannot cope with messy real-world input
A model reaches a working version faster — a good way to write the script, a poor way to be it
Scripts require a deployment process the model avoids
items.explain: Deterministic work done by a model is slower, costs per run, and is occasionally wrong in ways nobody checks because it is usually right.

items.q: What is the honest base rate for a shared custom assistant?
options: Most get adopted once colleagues have seen a demonstration
Its author uses it and nobody else does
Adoption depends mainly on how well the instructions are written
items.explain: Colleagues have their own habits and did not ask for it. A prompt in a shared document often gets more use and costs nothing to maintain.
